nutshell: Unsupervised person ReID methods typically represent each pseudo-label cluster with a single 'uni-proxy' (e.g. the centroid), which gets biased and confused by intra-class variance and inter-class similarity. DCMIP instead maintains several discrepant cluster proxies (updated by different rules) that collaboratively represent a cluster for intra-class compactness, plus per-instance proxies used for global (not just in-batch) hard negative mining to increase inter-class separation.
contributions: Discrepant Cluster Proxies (DCP): maintains M proxies per cluster, each updated with a different sampling rule (mean/random/hardest instance feature in the mini-batch) rather than a single centroid uni-proxy, using them as hard positive samples in a cluster contrastive loss to collaboratively pull instances together.

Multi-Instance Proxies (MIP) with global hard negative mining: stores per-instance feature proxies for every cluster in a memory bank and mines the truly hardest negatives across the entire embedding space for an instance contrastive loss, instead of only mining hard negatives within the current mini-batch as prior work does.

Combining DCP and MIP (DCMIP, with instance-level loss phased in only after epoch 20) achieves new state-of-the-art unsupervised (no-label) mAP on both Market-1501 (86.7) and MSMT17 (40.9), with ablations isolating each component's individual contribution.
deficiencies: The optimal cluster-proxy update-design combination is dataset-specific and not derived automatically by the method: Market-1501 needs 'Mean+Hard' while MSMT17 needs 'Mean+Rand' (using 'Hard' collapses MSMT17 to 18.5 mAP per Table 3), so applying DCMIP to a new dataset appears to require re-searching this categorical hyperparameter rather than the method adapting to it.

The comparison against batch-hard-triplet and batch-hard-instance mining baselines (Table 2) fixes the cluster-loss weight λ=0.5 from epoch 21 in every row, but the paper doesn't show these baseline mining strategies re-tuned for their own optimal weighting/schedule - so part of MIP's reported advantage over batch-hard mining could reflect a hyperparameter setting favorable to MIP rather than a clean comparison of mining strategies alone.

All reported numbers (Tables 1-4) appear to be single-run results with no variance or multiple-seed reporting, despite some component-wise gains being under 1 mAP point (e.g., DCMIP vs. Baseline+DCP: +0.9 mAP on Market-1501).

The paper's own Discussion section concedes that using a fixed number of cluster proxies (two, uniformly across all clusters) is 'not the optimal solution' since clusters with different intra-class compactness would benefit from a dynamically-sized proxy count - an acknowledged limitation left entirely to future work rather than addressed in the current method.
notable: Instance proxies in the memory bank are directly replaced each mini-batch by the current batch's features (Eq. 9), rather than momentum-updated like the cluster proxies (Eq. 2) - a deliberate asymmetry to keep instance-level negatives maximally up-to-date, worth noting if reusing only part of this architecture. Also notable: the future-work direction the paper flags (a dynamic, per-cluster proxy count) substantially overlaps with MCRN [39], a prior method already cited in Related Work as maintaining multi-centroid cluster representations - so this isn't as unclaimed a research direction as the Discussion section implies.
